### 1. Cache Engineering for Agents (2610.28577)
- what: Proposes "cache engineering," where an agent drops selected KV entries from attention and repositions retained keys via RoPE rotation without re-prefilling, served by an AKV engine (extended radix tree, segment-batch attention) built on SGLang.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched). The paper's own text was reviewed, not a summary.
- key numbers: Tool-response rolling drop (keep latest 12 tool responses) gives avg score 53.1 vs 51.0 for Standard and avg cost 7.3 vs 11.2 cents on GPT-OSS-120B (Table 1). Cost reduction 27.7% vs Standard is averaged over 3 models × 4 benchmarks, and the GPT-OSS-120B ablation (Table 3) uses only 100 tasks per benchmark. Serving: 1.18× output throughput and 1.51× P95 latency at peak concurrency on 80 SWE-Verified tasks, 8×A800.
- code/weights: Code at https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV (stated in the abstract). No weights are needed; the engine is a modified SGLang v0.5.20 fork.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The cheapest transferable idea is the decision to drop old tool-response KV and keep reasoning and recent tool outputs. That is testable with models he already runs, if his stack exposes KV control, which a hosted API like Muninn's does not. Evidence is weak for him: most gains are single-run or small deltas on 100-task subsets (Table 3 and the RSI result are on 100 held-out tasks with no reported spread beyond Figure 9's ±1σ over three runs), and the 27.7% headline depends on the authors' own cost model that charges repos at cache-hit rates. The serving engine needs modified SGLang across eight A800s, so the system part stays out of reach.

### 1. LiFT: Loop Flow Transformers (2610.05538)
- what: Trains a looped DiT core where each loop is supervised at a point on a straight path from a detached initial velocity estimate to the flow-matching target, so loop count can be raised at inference without retraining.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched) — the paper text was provided directly, so this is a full read of the paper's own text.
- key numbers: L/2 R10 at 2 training loops has FID 20.30; at 8 inference loops and 50 steps, FID 10.95 at 28.24 TFLOPs, versus dense XL/2 at 14.30 (250 steps, 59.31 TFLOPs) and dense L/2 at 16.94 (50 steps, 8.07 TFLOPs). Dense L/2 at 250 steps reaches 15.74, so the headline is against a baseline run at much higher step count.
- code/weights: not stated (paper says "Coming Soon" in the header; no repository link in the text).
- practical: LOW
- why: Everything is ImageNet 256 class-conditional DiT at 50k-sample FID, trained for 500k updates on four H100s with a fixed 32.8B-token budget, so adopting it means training from scratch, which is out of reach for my setup. The paper's own Appendix B.4 and A.3 show single-run, untested FID differences near the plateaus, and the headline compares a looped model at 8 loops against dense baselines that must run 250 steps to reach their numbers. The depth-extrapolation finding (more loops at inference keep helping) is the one transferable idea, but I can only test it on a checkpoint I already have, and no such checkpoint is released.

### 1. Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement (2610.12369)
- what: Proposes Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP), a frozen, model-free robot policy written as code that tracks object and robot state from RGB and proprioception, developed offline by coding agents in a branch-and-accept loop on RoboDojo's 42 simulated bimanual tasks.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given, so I did not verify any external source)
- key numbers: 70.24% overall SR on RoboDojo vs 31.38% for the best leaderboard entry (PhysicalRSI, agent + VLA), and 27.96% for the best VLA; but the COAP policy was developed by Claude Opus 5.5 coding agents against the same benchmark's validation layouts, with 83% of code shared across tasks. Measured-state vs oracle-state success is 63% vs 83%. Test-vs-validation standard success is 74.9% vs 76.7%.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper mentions RoboDojo as a published benchmark [7] and says camera models and meshes are public, but gives no repository or release link for COAP.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism needs RoboDojo's simulator, its camera and mesh assets, and a coding agent to write and debug tens of thousands of lines of perception and manipulation code, none of which fits the reader's stack of text-memory agents, retrieval, or browser embeddings. The code-as-state idea is worth noting, but it is not transferable within weeks: the headline depends on an unreleased library, the leaderboard comparison is across different development effort, and the margins (about 39 points) are too large to trust without an independent replication. The reader's routing and memory work does not change because of this paper.

### 1. Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World (2610.14224)
- what: Proposes a recursive harness-optimization loop for LLM agents. Task-level recursion runs a label-free Propose–Probe–Compose step (parallel or sequential), and harnessing-level recursion keeps a library of adopted harnesses and lessons that guides later tasks.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: WorkBuddy-Bench Avg. for Gemini 3.5 Flash goes from 72.4 base to 76.5 at k=1 and 80.8 at k=5 (Code). Single-run deltas are mostly 2–5 points with SDs of 1–5 across three runs, and the paper's own leave-one-out and w/o-library ablations differ by 1–3 points. Judges are Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, with no agreement or calibration reported.
- code/weights: github.com/google-research/harness2 and harness2.github.io are stated in the paper. I did not check whether they run.
- practical: LOW
- why: The method needs many executor rollouts plus an Opus-class editor per task, and the headline depends on a 1–5 point margin that sits inside the reported SDs. I could use the library-and-lessons idea and the "verify workspace facts after copying a component" rule, but the expensive loop and the unvalidated LLM-judge scores don't meet the bar for a design change this month.

### 1. Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation (2610.14162)
- what: Trains a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to turn text into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete codes, then a ~100M transformer generates each level in parallel, so generation takes K≈8–32 steps instead of hundreds of denoising passes.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, only the GitHub repo https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm stated inside the paper)
- key numbers: LM1B 12 NFE vs DUO 128 NFE, with Gen. PPL 93.05 vs 97.30 at matched-ish entropy (4.31 vs 4.30) and 21× wall-clock speedup (Fig. 1/5). XSum ROUGE-L 28.0 at 8 NFE vs AURORA-LM 26.6 at 128 NFE (no guidance). Sudoku hard 86.1% vs FMLM+ 81.3%, using 12 vs 16 NFE.
- code/weights: GitHub repo https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm is stated in the paper; weights not explicitly stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The method needs a separately trained tokenizer plus a generator trained for 100k–350k steps on 13–127B token positions, and the speed claims are wall-clock on an H100 at batch 16 with baselines the authors partly sampled themselves, so it is not something he can run on his stack within weeks. The single-run, one-seed-per-setting results and the MBR gains (which spend the saved NFE back) weaken the headline comparison, and the "shared vocabulary" of coarse concepts and hierarchy does not run on his remex/remax or memory components; the only transferable idea is that coarse-first, parallel-per-level decoding could inform a future draft/routing design, not something to adopt now.

### 1. TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing (2610.12242)
- what: Proposes a serving runtime (on SGLang 0.5.1) for token-level LLM routing that hosts each model in a subserver, adds a route-send-receive API, a handoff-resume "pending" state, and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold comes from a DTMC throughput model.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: 2.01–64.15× throughput over the "stronger" baseline across 15 algorithm–workload combos; R2R at concurrency 4 goes 89.62 → 244.56 tok/s vs official code (Table 2), and 145.30 → 244.56 vs LLM-only; ablation at N=8: delayed batching adds 1.25× (296.86 → 372.48), async adds ~1.29× (230.79 → 296.86).
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter); model weights are public Qwen3 and R2R checkpoints, not new weights.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The headline 64× comes from weak baselines (official CITER/Co-LLM engines without continuous batching, a 3.46 tok/s Co-LLM run), while the fair comparison against LLM-only is 1.5–2.7×. The runtime is a fork of SGLang on 8×A100 with two-GPU TP and CUDA MPS, so it doesn't fit his single-box setup as-is, and the routing algorithms here are token-level 0.6B/32B pairs he doesn't run. The transferable idea is the delayed-batching threshold and the handoff-resume "pending" state for any multi-model decode loop he might build; I'd cap at MEDIUM and only act on those two ideas, not the system.

### 1. BizBench: Unveiling Hidden Challenges in Deploying Long-Horizon Agents for Real-World Business (2610.20424)
- what: Introduces a 50-task, multi-turn benchmark over a reconstructed payments-company environment (789 documents, 601 discoverable tools, a user simulator) that scores goal attainment, process compliance, and protection checks deterministically, so intermediate constraint violations count against a run.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, the paper's own arXiv id is 2610.20424)
- key numbers: Strict success: Claude Opus 5 64.0%, GPT-6 Sol 61.3%, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 43.3%, Qwen3.5-9B 0.0%. Goal-vs-strict gap for Qwen3.8-27B is 42.0% vs 32.7%. Tool-call cap at 2.0× Golden drops DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash strict success from 43.3% to 26.7%. Single run per task for the two top models; three runs for the rest.
- code/weights: GitHub https://github.com/ant-intl/BizBench and Hugging Face https://huggingface.co/datasets/ant-intl/BizBench are stated in the paper.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The strongest transferable finding is the evaluation design: a run that reaches the goal but breaches a reserve floor or acts before approval is scored as a failure, and the paper shows outcome-only grading would overstate validity. The tool-call-cap and repeated-read analysis is directly useful for auditing Muninn's delegation overhead. It is not a routing or memory method, though, and the benchmark needs the paper's payments environment, so the immediate use is a test-design idea rather than something to run as is. The "Golden trace" tool-call ratio is also a useful budget reference for cost tracking. Its results rest on 50 tasks with single runs for the top models and on a simulator that is itself an LLM, so the margins among mid-tier models are soft.

- what: Introduces a 50-task, multi-turn benchmark over a reconstructed payments-company environment (789 documents, 601 discoverable tools, a user simulator) that scores goal attainment, process compliance, and protection checks deterministically, so intermediate constraint violations count against a run.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, the paper's own arXiv id is 2610.20424)
- key numbers: Strict success: Claude Opus 5 64.0%, GPT-6 Sol 61.3%, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 43.3%, Qwen3.5-9B 0.0%. Goal-vs-strict gap for Qwen3.8-27B is 42.0% vs 32.7%. Tool-call cap at 2.0× Golden drops DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash strict success from 43.3% to 26.7%. Single run per task for the two top models; three runs for the rest.
- code/weights: GitHub https://github.com/ant-intl/BizBench and Hugging Face https://huggingface.co/datasets/ant-intl/BizBench are stated in the paper.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The strongest transferable finding is the evaluation design: a run that reaches the goal but breaches a reserve floor or acts before approval is scored as a failure, and the paper shows outcome-only grading would overstate validity. The tool-call-cap and repeated-read analysis is directly useful for auditing Muninn's delegation overhead. It is not a routing or memory method, though, and the benchmark needs the paper's payments environment, so the immediate use is a test-design idea rather than something to run as is. The "Golden trace" tool-call ratio is also a useful budget reference for cost tracking. Its results rest on 50 tasks with single runs for the top models and on a simulator that is itself an LLM, so the margins among mid-tier models are soft.

### 1. Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm (2610.40564)
- what: Recasts pretraining, midtraining, SFT, and binary-reward RL (MaxRL/REINFORCE/TailRL) as weighted maximum-likelihood fitting to a mixture of static data and model-generated success-conditioned targets, then trains one mixed-data trainer (asynchronous generator plus buffer) instead of staged pipelines.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, the arXiv id 2610.40564 is the source). The text includes appendices, so the experimental details were checked.
- key numbers: Controlled 124M-parameter puzzle task: best unified configs beat the best staged reference on Base accuracy (Fig. 4) and reach higher best-compute accuracy at larger budgets, but Table 9 shows the staged reference at 24.54% Base pass@1 with two seeds averaged. Real-world 0.76B math: 0% mixing (RL-only, unified trainer) gives Math pass@1 24.75% vs staged 24.16%, and the Math gap is within what the paper treats as noise. Coding after subsequent RL: unified 5% mixing gets HumanEval+ pass@1 24.96 vs staged 22.94, on a 164-problem benchmark with single runs.
- code/weights: GitHub https://github.com/yudasong/unified-training and Hugging Face https://huggingface.co/sfanm/unified-training are listed in the abstract. I did not verify that either resolves or contains the trainer.
- practical: LOW
- why: The usable idea is small: a token-weighted CE loss where RL correct samples get weight 1/p̂ and incorrect ones get 0, mixed into one batch with static data. That is a few lines on top of a trainer, but the paper's headline needs an asynchronous multi-GPU trainer (24 and 16 GPUs in the cited runs) and a 124M/0.76B model trained from scratch, neither of which he runs. Evidence is weak on the real-world side: most headline deltas are a few points from single-run or two-seed averages on 164 to 1024 items, and the paper itself says the best mixture is not identified. The part he could test in weeks is the loss shape on an existing SFT/RL loop, not the unified-training claim.

### 1. PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations (2610.37381)
- what: Adds a lightweight Physical Dynamics Module (50 learned queries over intermediate VLM features, ~57M params) that predicts future RGB/depth/flow latents, with a frozen video world model as auxiliary supervision, so the action expert gets physical tokens without generating video at control time.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given in the supplied text, and the review is based on that text only)
- key numbers: Held-out RoboCOIN future-feature MSE improves only 1.32% over direct-only (0.6439 to 0.6354, bootstrap CI [0.71, 1.89]); benchmark averages are 99.3% LIBERO vs 99.1% Qwen-RobotManip, 93.6% RoboTwin vs 93.2%, 81.5% SimplerEnv vs 80.8%. Gaps are about 0.2 to 0.7 points, all from single runs.
- code/weights: not stated in the paper text (no repository or checkpoint link appears).
- practical: LOW
- why: The core is a 4B VLA trained on 1.2M+ trajectory corpora and 40k to 150k-update fine-tunes, which is infrastructure you cannot run within weeks. The one transferable idea, probing intermediate-layer features for future-state prediction, is only a 1.3% held-out gain, and the benchmark margins sit within what single-seed runs would show. The subtask and ECoT results (for example, +0.30 points subtask conditioning, and ECoT generation at inference giving no gain) do suggest that inference-time generation is not worth its cost, which is a small design note for Muninn's routing.

- what: Alternates evolutionary search over textual multi-agent workflow prompts with SFT of a single Qwen3.6-27B on its own orchestrator/subagent traces, reporting two RSI cycles on research-style tasks.

- key numbers: Test win rate vs base rises 53.9% → 69.9% over two cycles; multi-agent student 68.3% vs single-agent student 64.0% at ~1.4× more processed tokens. ### 1. Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To (2610.11765)
- what: Defines "no-thinking" as a response-level property, splitting each output into pre-answer text T and final answer A, then measures Empty-Thinking Rate (ETR), an embedding-based Question–Pre-answer Relevance (QRel.), and a GPT-5.5 judge's Explicit Inference Rate (EIR) across six models, six benchmarks, and six prompt modes.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given in the supplied text)
- key numbers: Open-ended M2 (native Think-Off) EIR 99.69%, M5 (strict answer-only) 62.00%; Opus 4.8 judge gives 98.55% / 61.02%, so the judge-family check agrees. Strict prompting raises mean ETR from near zero to ~40% at a cost of ~15 accuracy points on open-ended tasks. Human binary agreement with GPT-5.5 is 98.8%.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper mentions "evaluation artifacts" and per-example annotations, but gives no repository or release link in the supplied text.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The Bool < MCQ < Open ordering is consistent across two judges, four encoders, and human labels, and it gives a concrete routing signal: Boolean or candidate-visible formats are cheap to answer directly, and open generation is not. ### 1. RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models (2610.13912)
- what: A framework that uses a learned world-model predictor to rank candidate actions before execution, then gates retention of updated policy and predictor pairs across update cycles, tested on code repair, GUI tasks, lab planning, and reaction optimization.
- read: full (text supplied in message, arXiv 2610.13912)
- key numbers: Code repair (200 CodeContests tasks, 3 seeds, 4 candidates per round): static verifier 26.3% → fixed world-model selection 29.2% (paired +2.83 pp, 95% CI [+0.17, +5.50]) → adapted predictor 31.2% (+2.0 pp, no interval reported). Chemistry: 96.15% vs 82.16% for Bayesian optimization at 40 experiments, with no spread reported.
- code/weights: GitHub repo stated (github.com/Gen-Verse/RSI-Anything). The "Models" link actually points to a Hugging Face dataset path. The W1 predictor and the 4B lab policy are not clearly released.
- practical: LOW
- why: The one transferable piece is ranking four coder proposals with a small learned execution-outcome predictor, which could be tried on Muninn's code subagents within weeks. But the headline gain has a lower CI bound near zero, the adaptation gain has no interval, and the GUI, lab, and chemistry results are single runs with no variance, so the evidence is weak. The retention and pair-gate mechanism, which is the paper's main contribution, has no reported ablation against ungated updates, and the predictor training depends on large execution-labelled data.

### 1. The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents (2610.36077)
- what: Builds a capability tree over 28 training benchmarks, evolves module-based Harnesses per node with a frozen Claude Opus 5 backbone, and routes tasks among those Harnesses with an agent-based router.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: Train mean 39.06 → 73.16 and Unseen 37.45 → 63.61 for Base vs. Iteration 4 (single backbone, single run per cell). Module-only Capability Tree (Sim) 56.95/47.26 vs. Global 53.04/42.92 after one iteration. Relevant module addition raises Base 39.06 → 58.45 vs. +1.02 for an irrelevant one. Routing: full self-router 71.27/60.96 vs. Oracle 73.16/63.61.
- code/weights: GitHub (https://github.com/InfRec-Cardinal/The-Trinity) and project page (https://trinity-rsi.github.io/) are stated. Backbone is a closed model (Claude Opus 5), so the headline numbers cannot be reproduced without API access to that model.
- practical: LOW
- why: The method is a multi-stage pipeline (world generation, verifier pools, host-validated module admission, six-protocol Harness library) that needs heavy orchestration and a frontier backbone, so it is out of stack for Muninn's cheap-subagent routing. The routing result is the closest fit, but it routes among Harnesses built for this benchmark suite on one large backbone, and the paper reports no run-to-run variance, so the 1–5 point gaps (e.g. Sim vs. Real, Iteration 3 vs. 4) are not reliable evidence. The idea of routing on capability requirements plus logged cost/outcome is worth borrowing as a design pattern, but the paper gives no evidence it works with small models.

- what: Proposes replacing the DRAM-then-SSD tiered KV cache hierarchy with peer DRAM and NVMe placement behind a unified 64-bit address space, with write-time session-contiguous layout, GDS streaming into a bounded GPU window, and dual-queue scheduling. Implemented in SGLang.

- key numbers: Opus 4.5 SWE-bench Verified 70.0 baseline vs 74.8 best EoCC (48K/36K→24K/18K range) and 70.2 under SAC with median peak live context of 8–9K; RULER mean recall 62.5→95.7 (Opus) with 16K total limit; the cost multiples (2.2x–8.8x on long-horizon, 6.5x–54.6x on long-input) rest on an estimated "optimized retail cost" formula with an assumed r=0.20 context factor, not measured billing.
- code/weights: none stated in the paper. Harnesses are described as mini-swe-agent (released) and a generalized mini-agent (not released as far as the text says). - practical: MEDIUM

- what: Proposes collective experience learning (CEL), implemented as FERT (failure-guided retrieval via S-DTW over successful fleet trajectories, then priority-weighted flow-matching fine-tuning) plus FATS (a fault-tolerant async data/control plane on RLinf), evaluated on five real AgiBot G2 manipulation tasks.

- what: Introduces a 56-task benchmark, built by 42 physicists from their own research, where agents must review literature, plan, run computations or experiments, and write a manuscript, graded by deterministic verifiers plus blocker and non-blocker rubrics judged by a reviewer agent.

- key numbers: Best configuration Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code) reaches 27.4% Pass@1 (46 of 168 rollouts) with a 95% CI of roughly [17.9, 36.9]; GPT-6 Astra (max) 23.2%, so the top two are statistically inseparable per Table 8. - what: Adds an implicit spatial-alignment loss (projecting multi-layer PaliGemma visual tokens via gated fusion onto OmniVGGT features) to π0.5 during both continual pre-training on ~1.7M curated robot episodes and post-training, with state dropout; inference architecture is unchanged.

### 1. Meta² : Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents (2611.05139)
- what: Learns an offline textual "Meta-Skill" from A/B/C rollout contrasts (no evolver / evolver guided by the current Meta-Skill / evolver with verifier info), then freezes it and uses it to guide KEEP-or-EVOLVE decisions at checkpoints inside each task run, with edits discarded when the run ends.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: Terminal-Bench 2.1 (GPT-5.6-Terra, mean@5, 60 test tasks): 81.00% vs NexAU seed 66.33% and best baseline Meta-Harness 73.33%. DeepSWE 1.1 (mean@3, 75 test tasks): 44.44% vs seed 34.67%. Ablation on DeepSWE: 44.44 vs 36.44 with no Meta-Skill and 35.56 self-distilled. Standard deviations across repeats are 0.91 and 0.77 pp, but these are over a single test split with one backbone for each comparison.
- code/weights: project page https://meta-square.github.io/ is listed; no code repository or Meta-Skill artifact is stated in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism is worth borrowing as a design pattern (frozen guidance plus task-local, discarded edits, with KEEP as a first-class action), but the headline needs GPT-5.6-Terra, E2B sandboxes, and the Terminal-Bench/DeepSWE harnesses, none of which he runs. The paper also admits the A/B/C contrasts are not causal, and the ablations are single-run deltas on 60–75 tasks. The 4.0 and 8.9 pp gains from contrastive learning sit within the gap a single unvalidated split can produce. This is an out-of-stack harness-evolution system, so per the E-01 and E-05 rules it stays LOW even though a KEEP-by-default checkpoint policy might be tested cheaply on Muninn's subagent routing.

- what: Describes CoworkOS, a harness that splits a Main agent (decides strategy), a Coordinator runtime (durable delegation, messaging, jobs), and Subagents, plus shared-artifact editing, persistent workspaces and memory; evaluated on 12 benchmarks and an RSI post-training loop on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

- key numbers: Tool Use average 55.22 vs DeepSeek Harness 55.31 and OpenHands 51.33; Productivity 57.54 vs DSH 56.13; RSI post-training average 33.19 to 42.95 over five rounds, with the single-run per-round changes unreplicated.

- practical: LOW
